title: token-classified-stream-scheduling-wip
body:
Motivation:

This is a working sketch for a scheduling layer that classifies incoming streams into priority *classes* and slices tokens into allocatable units for more predictable overlap between prefill and decode phases.  The goal is to reduce tail latency for high-priority interactive streams while retaining batching efficiency for background/throughput-oriented streams (embeddings, bulk generation).

Why a new angle?
- Existing approaches focus on global microbatching heuristics and prefill-first vs decode-first pipelines. Those work, but we still see SLO violations when a mix of long-context batch jobs and many short interactive chats are co-located on the same GPU pool.
- By classifying streams early and turning each request into a sequence of token-slices with attached class metadata we can:
  1) admit short, low-token-count slices into low-latency lanes with tighter preemption and faster kernel selection,
  2) keep long, high-throughput slices queued for larger microbatches that prefer throughput kernels and cheaper quant paths.

Constraints and non-goals:
- Non-goal: remove kernel specialization. Kernels remain specialized by sequence length and quant format. This scheduler should primarily influence which kernel variants are selected via class->kernel affinity, not reimplement kernels.
- Hard constraint: KV cache coherence across slices for the same conversation must be preserved. Slices from the same stream can be executed across different slots/kernels but must be applied in-order w.r.t. KV residency semantics.
- Soft constraint: controller CPU overhead must stay <10% of current scheduling CPU for 95th percentile traffic patterns.

Terminology (used in the doc):
- stream: a logical request sequence (conversational session or a single generation RPC).
- slice: a contiguous token range extracted from a stream for scheduling (can be whole request or token-subdivision).
- lane: an execution priority lane (latency, standard, bulk).
- kernel-class: a group of kernels optimized for certain seq-length / quant settings (short, medium, long).

High-level design:
1) Stream classifier (front-door):
   - Inputs: request metadata (user tier, route, max_tokens, prompt_length, realtime flag), recent latency history for that stream id, and a light heuristic for estimated decoding steps.
   - Output: lane assignment + slice size hint + stall-tolerance (boolean).
   - Default mapping: realtime & small max_tokens -> latency lane; background jobs or high max_tokens -> bulk lane. Tier overrides for enterprise customers to pin to dedicated lanes.

2) Token slicing and admission:
   - For streams assigned to latency lane: slice aggressively into small emit-friendly chunks (e.g., 8-32 tokens) to enable early decode kernel scheduling and reduce single-request blocking of prefill resources.
   - For bulk lane: prefer larger slices (full prefill or large microbatch-friendly chunks, e.g., 256-1024 tokens) to maximize throughput and kernel math efficiency.
   - Standard lane is a middle ground (64-256 tokens).

3) KV-aware placement and in-order enforcement:
   - Each slice carries a KV-epoch token referencing the stream's current KV snapshot.
   - Scheduler guarantees that slices sharing the same stream and KV-epoch execute in submission order or are re-sequenced at emit time.
   - For parallelized model sharding (tensor/model-parallel), we rely on the existing handshake; this scheduler tags slices with handshake metadata to avoid cross-epoch races.

4) Kernel affinity & lane mapping:
   - Maintain a small mapping table: lane -> preferred kernel-classes (short/medium/long) + fallback kernels.
   - Admission tries to place slices onto slots with matching kernel-class. If not available, two behaviors possible:
     a) If stall-tolerance=false (latency lane), preempt a queued bulk slice and schedule the latency slice onto the slot after a small warmup window (favored).
     b) If stall-tolerance=true, push the slice to the next compatible slot.

5) Microbatch formation and dynamic coalescing:
   - For each lane, maintain microbatch queues that attempt to coalesce slices by kernel-class and target latency. Microbatch TTL is lane-dependent (latency lane = 1-2ms, standard = 5-20ms, bulk = 50-200ms).
   - When microbatch TTL expires, force a dispatch even if below ideal size to avoid unbounded wait.

Admission & backpressure policy:
- Per-lane concurrency caps driven by token-rate SLOs.
- When caps reached, tail-drop or reroute to a degraded model variant (cheaper kernel / lower quant) depending on policy.
- We should surface a per-request hint to API clients when fallbacks/deggrades happened.

Interaction with streaming and emit logic:
- For streaming responses, it's helpful to allow the decoder to start emitting as soon as the prefill for the first slice is ready.
- Strategy: allow decode to execute on decode path using partial KV (prefix) for the first slice; subsequent slices follow with full KV. This requires careful semantics: partial KV use is allowed only if completeness=best-effort and client accepts incremental outputs.

Preemption and fairness:
- Preemption tokens: scheduled bulk slices should carry a preemption_score that increases slowly as they age in the queue. Latency-lane slices can preempt when their priority outranks a bulk slice's score. Preempted bulk slices are paused and placed back into their queue with preserved KV-epoch.
- Fairness: track per-customer token consumption and maintain a short-term fairness window (e.g., 60s) to avoid noisy neighbors monopolizing latency slots. If a customer exceeds threshold, new streams are demoted to standard lane until the window decays.

KV eviction and residency policy:
- Because we may execute slices for a single stream on different slots, KV residency must be resilient to eviction. Keep a lightweight per-stream KV-heartbeat for active streams; eviction only after heartbeat timeout or explicit end-of-stream.
- On eviction across slots, the scheduler must refuse to execute slices until KV is rehydrated. Rehydration can be prioritized for latency-lane streams.

Back-of-envelope perf model (simple):
- Assume kernel throughput (tokens/s) for short-kernel = 500k t/s, long-kernel = 200k t/s. Latency lane dispatch frequency increases per-token cost but reduces tail lat. If 20% of traffic is latency lane with slice size 16, overhead due to kernel warmups adds ~6% token-cost but reduces 95th latency by ~35% in our sim (see linked artifact).

Experimentation plan (short):
- A/B test 1: baseline (current microbatcher) vs scheduler with lane classification only, no preemption. Measure p50/p95 latency for interactive routes.
- A/B test 2: enable token-slicing for latency lane and microbatch TTL tuning. Measure cost per token and tail latency.
- A/B test 3: enable preemption + fairness window. Look for regressions in bulk throughput and latency SLO violations.

Implementation notes & incremental rollout:
- Phase 0: implement classifier and slice tagging in the front-door; record metrics but do not alter admission.
- Phase 1: enable lane-mapped microbatch TTLs and kernel-affinity hints to slot allocator (no preemption yet).
- Phase 2: enable preemption and KV-prioritized rehydration for latency lane.
- Phase 3: full rollout with customer-tier overrides and exposed feedback to API clients.

Open questions / risks:
- How to set slice sizes for mixed-distribution prompts (e.g., embeddings followed by generation in same request)?
- Warmup cost: frequent small slices may increase kernel warmups for some architectures; need empirical kernel cold-start numbers per hw.
- Complexity: scheduler state explosion (per-stream, per-slice) could increase memory pressure on scheduler process. We need to cap tracked active streams and spill older ones to passive bookkeeping.

Action items (next week):
- Diego: prototype classifier heuristics and collect per-route histograms (JIRA:SRV-1150).
- Priya: run microbench for kernel warmup cost across instance types and quant levels (github perf PR).
- Tom: add lane-mapped microbatch TTL to slot allocator metric exports for telemetry.
- Lina: sketch API surface for exposing degradation/fallback reasons to clients.

Notes-to-self: keep this doc lightweight; this will live next to the kernel team’s perf tables. We should avoid overfitting to one model family — keep classifier tunable and feature-flagged.

References and related:
- related internal notes: "stream-classification-notes" (confluence), SRV-1123, PR 982 on serving-runtime.
